arguments.content:
Caring for a Maltese coat properly keeps it silky, white, and free of painful mats — the full bath-to-blow-dry process takes about 1.5 to 2.5 hours depending on coat length and how tangled it is, so plan accordingly.

1. Gather your products and tools. You'll need: a gentle, whitening or brightening dog shampoo (such as Pure Paws White Shampoo, Chris Christensen White on White, Arterra Whitening Shampoo, or a mild hypoallergenic oatmeal shampoo for sensitive skin); a high-quality moisturizing or detangling conditioner (top picks: The Stuff, IC Dog Detangler, Arterra Reconstructor, or Chris Christensen After Bath); a leave-in conditioner or conditioning spray (e.g., The Stuff diluted in a spray bottle, or Ice On Ice); an undercoat rake and a slicker brush (soft-pin for Maltese's fine hair); a metal greyhound comb with fine and wide spacing; a pin brush; a high-velocity dryer or a variable-temperature stand/hand dryer; cotton balls (for the ears); a non-slip mat for the tub; and a dampening spray bottle.

2. Brush the coat thoroughly before any water touches it. Using the slicker brush and then the metal comb, work through the entire coat section by section, starting at the feet and moving upward. Water tightens existing tangles into hard mats, so this pre-bath brushing is the single most important step — expect 20–40 minutes on a full-coat Maltese.

3. Prepare the bath area. Place a non-slip mat in the tub, put cotton balls gently in the dog's ears to keep water out, and dilute your shampoo and conditioner in separate squeeze bottles (a 4:1 water-to-product ratio for conditioner is typical) so you can spread them evenly through the coat.

4. Wet the coat completely with lukewarm water. Use a sprayer or pitcher to saturate the fur right down to the skin — a Maltese's dense coat resists surface wetting. Keep the water temperature consistent and avoid the face for now.

5. Apply shampoo and wash. Work the whitening or gentle shampoo into the coat from neck to tail, lathering well and scrubbing gently with your fingertips (never nails). Wash the face last with a damp washcloth or a tearless puppy shampoo, then rinse thoroughly — any shampoo residue left behind will attract dirt and cause itching.

6. Apply conditioner. Work the moisturizing conditioner through the coat, focusing on the ends and any areas prone to tangling. Leave it on for 3–5 minutes (per product instructions) to penetrate — Maltese hair has no undercoat, so conditioning is what keeps it from becoming brittle and breaking.

7. Rinse, rinse, and rinse again. This takes longer than you think: rinse until the water runs completely clear with zero slippery feel. Residual conditioner is a leading cause of dull coats and rapid re-matting. A final cool-water rinse helps close the cuticle and add shine.

8. Remove excess water. Squeeze (don't twist) water out of the coat with your hands, then blot with an absorbent microfiber towel or a absorbent "turbo towel." The coat should be damp, not dripping, before drying begins.

9. Blow dry while brushing. This is the step that makes or breaks the coat. Using a high-velocity dryer (or a hand dryer on low heat/cool setting, held at least 12 inches away), dry the coat section by section while following immediately with the pin brush or slicker brush, brushing in the direction of hair growth. Work from the back legs forward and finish last around the face (which the dog will dislike most). Keep the dryer moving and check coat temperature frequently to prevent overheating the skin. Expect 40–75 minutes for a full blow dry — rushing here is exactly how mats form overnight.

10. Final comb-out and finishing spray. Once the coat is completely dry, run the metal comb through every section to catch any tangles the dryer created, then apply a light mist of leave-in conditioner or detangling spray and give a final pass with the pin brush. A tiny pinch of coat oil or a light dusting of cornstarch-based grooming powder at the skin can absorb oil between baths.

Done right, this routine every 1–2 weeks (with light brushing several times a week in between) will keep your Maltese's coat mat- and tangle-free — budget about two hours per bath session, and the coat will reward you with that signature flowing, bright-white finish.
